           knights. They often fall prey to it, but almost nev-
           er use it. The Gamemaster should generally describe
      the effects seen, saying: “Fire breaks out in a circle around the
      knight” or make simple statements, such as: “You have been
      blessed.” There is no need to describe how magic works, or even
      to state it is being used.
        Magic should never dominate the game. Gamemasters
      should feel free to make magic take whatever form they wish, as
      long as it is subtle. Establish a mood with magic: let palaces glow
      from a warm internal light, serve exotic and intoxicating wines
      from Cathay, have a dove deliver a letter from heaven. Magic is
      an essential plot device for Gamemasters. A magical event or
      curse can form the basis for an adventure.
        Magic in this game is for purposes of roleplaying, not for
      cartoon violence. Paladin magic imitates the traditional magi-
      cal effects found in the epics, rather than comic-book flash-bang
      spells. Fate and luck are important components of magic, not
      just spells and spell casters. The fundamental laws of society,
      such as loyalty or hospitality, are enforced by the decrees of fate,
      and enter the realm of magic.
        To make magic work, the Gamemaster simply says that it
      works; there is no way for knights to defend against it. This is
      extremely powerful, and Gamemasters are urged to use it spar-
      ingly and not corrupt the game by using magic at every turn. It
      ought to be used as special effects instead of major plot devices.

      users. We find swords that are better than usual, horns that can
      only be sounded by a specific person, the water of a fountain
      that inspires feelings of hatred or love, or a castle that revolves
      around its axis. They are sources of awe, wonder and fear for nor-
      mal people.

  potent, partially because of its very mystery. Paladin magic is
  dangerous because it is hidden and subtle. Your character knows
  that magic is more likely to drive him mad or age him a century
  in a day than to toast him with a lightning bolt.
     People accept the world of magic as a normal part of the
  great unknowable reality. They have heard about, and per-
  haps seen, magical objects like the sword Durendal and the
  Oriflamme. But men do not hope to understand it.
     Magicians are not to be trusted. Everyone knows some rea-
  son for this, though the reasons vary depending on the point of
  view of the observer. Some mistrust them because they can alter
  reality, or talk to the dead, or can tell what the weather is going
  to be and change it if they don’t like it. Other people dislike ma-
  gicians because they believe that all occult powers come from the
  Devil. Some don’t like anyone who is strange, and magicians have
  access to the unknowable; what is not known cannot be trusted.

minor magical healing or divination skills. There are even the
      rare wizard-knights, like Sir Maugis.
        Below, we discuss these different magical manifestations
      from a Gamemaster perspective, before addressing the issue of
      player access to certain types of divine aid.
      Divine Magic

        The most important source of magic is divine power from
      Heaven, which the Christian priests try to channel down to
      earth for the sake and salvation of all.
      Prayers
        Priests, monks and pious hermits all try to attract the good-
      will of God and benefit from His infinite power. They do so by
      sacred rituals and prayers. Of course, ordinary folk also pray God
      for aid. Though divine aid is rare, it does sometimes happen. In
      game terms, God may manifest his power through miraculous
      events, such as healings, visions, or the appearance of angels.
      After the battle of Roncevaux, God helps his followers by
      stopping the course of the sun:
       See, an angel now comes again and speaks;

       Immediately he commanded the king:
       “Charlemagne, ride on, daylight will not fail you.
       You have, as God knows, lost the flower of Frankland;
       You can avenge yourself on this criminal race.”
       With these words the emperor mounted his horse.
       God performed a miracle for Charlemagne,
       For the sun remained where it was.

           — The Song of Roland, CLXXIX–CLXXX
        Whatever its manifestation, divine magic cannot backfire,
      nor can it be countered by faeries, spells or other forms of mag-
      ic. Against the maleficent forces of paganism (trolls, woodland
      sprites, sacred groves or enchanted springs) there are no better
      weapons than prayers.
      Sacred Places
        Chapels, churches, cathedrals, monasteries, abbeys, tombs
      of saints, pilgrimage sites and other sacred grounds are known
      to radiate more or less divine power. Over time, Christian rituals
      have permanently sanctified these places where the pure of heart
      have generously prayed for others, where a great miracle once
      happened, or where one or more relics are kept. This ambient
      holy magic can be felt by devout Christians praying at such plac-
      es. Therefore, a Player-knight receives a bonus when praying at
      a sacred place.
      Relics and Blessed Objects

        Similar to sacred places, some objects, called relics, are spe-
      cial to the Christian faith and permanently imbued with Divine
      magic. They are usually stored in a special shrine called reliquary

and displayed to the pious to be venerated, for their blessing may
  rub off on the truly faithful.
     Another common use of relics is to set them into armor or
  weapons in order to assist Christian knights in their combat with
  the forces of evil. Body parts of saints (bones, tears, blood, or
  hair) or objects they used to perform their blessed deeds (crosses,
  swords, staffs, cloaks, and books) may all qualify as relics. These
  sacred objects may confer a bonus to certain types of prayers. For
  example, a relic of St. Hubertus (the patron of hunters) may give
  +3 to prayers concerning a hunt or hunters. Or a knight wearing
  a small necklace containing a drop of St. Martin’s blood may add
  +1 to his score in Generous. For more examples and information
  on relics, see Chapter 12: Wealth and Treasure.
  Wizardly Magic
     Wizardly magic is opposed to the sacred supernatural.
  Ordinary people see it as “black magic,” used by wicked sorcer-
  ers who use it to gain power and manipulate their victims. They
  obtain their magic from arcane books, their knowledge of astrol-
  ogy, and magic objects which they use to cast powerful spells.
  Their magic sometimes produces effects that resemble God’s
  miracles, and because of this confusion, all magicians are deeply
  mistrusted.
  Wizards and Sorcerers

     Player-knights should never be magicians, since they would
  have a disruptive effect on the game. Wizards can be present in
  the game as NPCs, though. Chapter 16: Non-Player Characters
  presents magicians who play a role in the legends. Other exam-
  ples of magic-wielding characters are court astrologers, who can
  read the stars and (sometimes) predict the future. Whether their
  skills are really magic, or reliable, is up to the Gamemaster.
  Spells and Player-Knights
     Most magicians and sorceresses cast their magic spells with
  the help of an enchanted object. Some use a spell book describ-
  ing intricate rituals, others use the arcane knowledge of magic
  herbs.
     Some spells cast on Player-knights have a force equal to the
  result of 1d20, which is rolled when the spell is cast. Great magi-
  cians like Atlantes or Maugis may add +5, or even +10, to their
  roll.
     For example, if a magician casts a Sleep spell on a Player-
  knight, the Gamemaster rolls a1d20 and compares the result to
  the victim’s resistance (if any); usually an attribute, trait, or pas-
  sion. For a Sleep spell, the Gamemaster might allow the victim
  to roll against Energetic or CON as resistance.
     Examples of magic rituals that can be found in the epics
  include curing illness or wounds, understanding animal speech,
  opening locks, long distance travel, invisibility, casting curses,
  creating food and drink, finding objects or thieves, restoring sex-
  ual potency, inducing love or hate, conjuring demons, creating
  mists or fogs, and finding plants.

They charge through the gate, eager to fight.
       Then a mist begins to fall from the sky
       so that none of the men can see to ride.
       The Franks have no way to defend their lives
       while the enemies attack the tents with fierce cries.

       They lead off the horses and kill the squires,
       they carry off the food from the kitchen fires
       and kill the chief steward before they retire.
           — The Coronation of Louis, LVII

      Conjuring Demons
        A frequently-used alternative to casting spells is to conjure
      a demon, which is bound to the magician’s will and commanded
      to produce magic for them. Conjuring demons is generally seen
      as black magic, though Christian wizards and good faeries are
      known to practice this type of magic, showing that it is possible
      to harness evil in the service of good.
        Demons can produce any sort of magical effect, but to
      command them a wizard needs a few things: he must perform a
      specific ritual, call the demon by his exact name (like Astaroth,
      Beliel, Draginazz or Marax) and, finally, bind it to his will.
      Conjuring demons from hell is not without risks, because if
      the last step fails, the demon attacks his would-be master. For
      more information on demons, see Chapter 18: Opponents and
      Creatures.
      Atlantes conjured demons to build his invisible fortress:
       Hell’s demons by enchantment built
       The whole thing in a single day.
           — Orlando Innamorato, 2.3.XXVII
      Enchanted Items

        Items possessing magical qualities are called enchanted. For
      some specific examples, see Chapter 12: Wealth and Treasure.

        A frequently-used alternative to casting spells is to conjure
      a demon, which is bound to the magician’s will and commanded
      to produce magic for them. Conjuring demons is generally seen
      as black magic, though Christian wizards and good faeries are
      known to practice this type of magic, showing that it is possible

title: Judicial Combats and Ordeals
leftColumn:
Astride their stallions, three white knights come
       Down from the ridge of lofty Aspremont
       And one by one pass each battalion;
       They do not speak and are addressed by none;
       They ride in haste until they reach the front.

           — Song of Aspremont, IX
      Judicial Combats and Ordeals

      In a trial by combat God helps justice to prevail:
       Huon advances to take the sword, because he is convinced
       his opponent surrenders. The noble young sir stretches
       out his hand, but the traitor lashes out and strikes him
       on the arm with such force that nigh three hundred rings
       of his mail burst: his arm would have been cut off, but
       God protected his champion.
           — Huon of Bordeaux, XVII
        At some point in your campaign, a Player-knight is likely
      to fight a trial by combat. Whether he acts as the champion for
      his lord or to defend the honor of a lady, the knight must defeat
      an opponent in a duel to prove who has God on their side. God
      protects the Just; therefore, if the Player-knight is defending the
      right (as determined by the Gamemaster), he may roll Just; on a
      success, add half the value of the roll to his armor (add his entire
      Just score on a critical). This bonus is cumulative with any oth-
      ers, and Inspiration may still be attempted.
        Example of a Trial by Combat: Sir Waldemar fights to re-
      fute the slanderous accusation that his sister committed adultery.
        Sir Waldemar rolls against his Just score. He gets a successful
      roll of 7. Assuming his sister is actually innocent (which only the
      Gamemaster knows for sure), Sir Waldemar’s armor score may be
      raised by 4 points (3½ rounded up) for the duration of the judicial
      combat. Whatever the outcome of the Just roll, he may also roll his
      Love [family] for Inspiration.
        The same rules may be applied for Player-knights submit-
      ting to an Ordeal (See Trial by Ordeal on page 222). Success at
      Just during a trial of Boiling Water or Hot Iron means that the
      character automatically passes the Valorous roll, and gains twice
      the benefit of healing. In a Proof of the Cross, the character’s
      STR roll is doubled to determine how long the character held
      up the weights.

       The Frankish people are second to none in strength; they
       conquer through God’s love, and they prevail through
       faith.
           — Ermold the Black, III

      try to convince him to convert to Christianity and become a
      friend rather than an enemy.

If they want to preserve their Honor, Saracens willing to con-
      vert need a good occasion to do so:
       “If God promotes the plans that I have made,
       In Him I’ll trust and Christian law obey;
       But for the length of this ferocious fray,
       While in the battle, I cannot change my faith.”
           — Song of Aspremont, III

        For the conversion attempt to be successful, both the knight
      and his pagan opponent must succeed at their Honor roll. If the
      knight wins the contest the pagan surrenders and agrees to be
      converted. The convert automatically acquires scores in Love
      [God] and Love [Charlemagne] equal to the Frankish knight’s
      successful Honor roll. At his baptism, his Christian godfather
      must choose a new name for him. Traditionally, the convert is
      then married to a Christian lady.
        If the pagan is victorious with a partial success for the
      Player-knight, he declines the offer to convert, but recognizes
      his opponent as a worthy and respected comrade. If the Player-
      knight fails the roll, the pagan sneers and insults him. If the
      Player-knight fumbles his Honor, the pagan instantly develops a
      Hatred against him equal to his own Honor score.
        If the pagan fails his Honor roll, he insults the knight and
      challenges him to a fight (or continues the fight already in prog-
      ress). If he fumbles the roll, he pretends to be willing to be bap-
      tized, but will break this promise at the first occasion and attack
      or betray the knight.
        Honorable converted pagans completely renounce their
      former beliefs and usually become excellent Christians. They
      may immediately benefit from prayers and other forms of di-
      vine aid.
      The miraculous conversion of Otuel, a valiant pagan knight:
       That instant a dove, white as snow, passed before Ro-
       land’s eyes and those of the entire army. It was the Holy
       Ghost in the shape of a dove. The bird spoke tender words
       at Otuel: “Go to Roland and do as he tells you.” Otuel
       replied: “I don’t know what my eyes behold, but my spirit
       and senses are transformed; what I loathed before now
       seems true to me. I will abandon my sword of my own free
       will and not out of fear. I shall no longer fight you, and for
       your sake shall I rally Charlemagne and his companions,
       even though I never imagined doing such a thing. The
       gods I worshiped now seem all worthless, as are those who
       serve them. From now on shall I call on Virgin Mary with
       all my heart, mother of Christ, to help and assist me.
         Roland heard these words and replied, smilingly: “Are
       these strong resolutions? Do they come from your heart?”
       Otuel replied: “Yes, it is nothing but the truth.” Then they
       embraced.
           — Karlamagnus Saga, 6.VI

title: Winning the Heart
leftColumn:
Whenever God wishes to communicate with his champi-
      ons, he sends an angel, a prophetic dream, or some other sort
      of sign. It could be a command, a warning, or some useful piece
      of information. A dream may reveal something hidden — like
      an opponent’s weakness, the hiding place of a treasure, a key, or
      an entrance to a faerie castle. Dreams and omens can be a subtle
      way for the Gamemaster to guide the players and give them a bit
      of advice or knowledge about future events, or they can simply
      whet the player’s appetite about upcoming adventures.
        To benefit from divine messages, a character first needs to
      succeed with a Love [God] roll to receive it. A critical success
      gives him +5 to the subsequent Religion roll.
        In most cases the message is obscure and ambiguous, so it
      needs to be interpreted carefully, preferably by a man of learning
      like a priest or a bishop. Hints about the correct meaning of the
      omen are only given to players if they or their advisor succeed
      with a Religion roll.
      The miracle of the sprouting lances:
       And then, some of the Christians were preparing their
       arms, the night before the battle, and they fixed their
       lances straight up in the ground, in the meadow by the
       bank of the river. And the following morning they found
       them with branches grown on them, and having bark
       and roots, namely, the lances of those who were about to
       receive the palm of victory and martyrdom for the faith
       of Christ, in the first line of battle.
           — Red Book of Hergest, ‘
            History of Charlemagne, X
        Note that the practice of oneiromancy (the interpretation
      of dreams) is officially forbidden for people outside the Church;
      but it is still widely practiced by hermits, witches, and astrologers
      at foreign courts. Apart from the obvious problems of interpreta-
      tion, the Church’s interdict is based on the knowledge that many
      false prophets use fake omens, visions and prophecies to rally the
      credulous and uneducated to their sinful causes. Knights should
      beware of dead people speaking to them in dreams, for demons
      and sorcerers send false dreams and prophecies to trick heroes.
      Charlemagne receives prophetic dreams:
       He dreamed he was at the main pass of Cize;
       In his hands he was holding his lance of ash.
       Count Ganelon seized it from his grasp;
       He broke it and brandished it with such violence
       That the splinters flew up to the sky.
       Charlemagne sleeps on without being roused.
       After this dream he had another vision:
       That he was in Frankland in his chapel at Aachen;
       In his right hand he is bitten by a vicious boar.
       From the direction of the Ardennes he saw a leopard
        coming;
       It attacks his body with great ferocity.

    Bounding and leaping towards Charlemagne.
    It tore the right ear of the first boar;
    Angrily it wrestles with the leopard.
    The Franks say there is a mighty battle;

    They do not know which of them will win it.

       — Song of Roland, LVI–LVII
     Example of an Omen: The Saxons will soon raid a Player-
  knight’s poorly-defended manor. In order to give the knight a
  chance to prepare himself, the Gamemaster asks the player to roll
  Love [God]. On a success, the knight wakes up to discover a gloomy
  and foreshadowing event: a wily fox has eaten all the ducks and
  chickens in the hen house, and all their eggs have turned into stones.
  Only the rooster survived, but it is bleeding badly and has lost most
  of its feathers.

Whenever God wishes to communicate with his champi-
      ons, he sends an angel, a prophetic dream, or some other sort
      of sign. It could be a command, a warning, or some useful piece

      gives him +5 to the subsequent Religion roll.

      needs to be interpreted carefully, preferably by a man of learning
      like a priest or a bishop. Hints about the correct meaning of the

        Note that the practice of oneiromancy (the interpretation
      of dreams) is officially forbidden for people outside the Church;
      but it is still widely practiced by hermits, witches, and astrologers
      at foreign courts. Apart from the obvious problems of interpreta-
      tion, the Church’s interdict is based on the knowledge that many
      false prophets use fake omens, visions and prophecies to rally the
      credulous and uneducated to their sinful causes. Knights should
      beware of dead people speaking to them in dreams, for demons
      and sorcerers send false dreams and prophecies to trick heroes.

An enamored pagan lady will gladly help her Frankish lover
      and his friends, and generates an Amor [knight] passion (see be-
      low). This includes helping them to escape from her father’s pris-
      on, betraying a pagan fortification to the Franks, or fleeing from
      home taking a relic or a treasure with her. In return, the lady
      expects to be baptized and married to her lover as soon as possi-
      ble. Should a Frankish lover betray her and not comply with her
      demands afterwards, the lady generates a Hate [knight] equal
      to her previous Amor score, and the Player-knight immediately
      loses 5 points of Honor and Love [God]. See the adventure The
      Pagan Lady (page 419) for an example of such a disgraceful ploy.

      with a knight, depending on the knight’s action (or inaction):
      passive infatuation and deliberate amor.
